newsitem.title: UK: Derivatives industry musters forces ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Derivatives industry musters forces ahead of EMU.

text.p: A shakeout of derivatives activity in London, sparked by intense competition, could leave the industry better placed to face the challenges of European economic and monetary union, industry observers said on Tuesday.

Tighter margins, cut-throat brokerage costs, and the high risk attached to trading in futures and options have led some banks to rethink their focus -- and the process is likely to continue in the run-up to EMU.

"It's like a tree in a storm, where the weaker parts get tossed out," said the head of a trading booth at a European brokerage. "With the EMU threat around the corner, firms want to scale back and regroup their energy to ensure they go into the single currency fighting fit."
Yamaichi International said last week it planned to close its futures and options section in London over the next month.
Also, NatWest Bank said on Monday that Martin Owen, chief executive of investment banking arm NatWest Markets, had resigned and that a major overhaul of the business was under way.
NatWest Markets in February disclosed it had lost 90 million pounds in interest rate options losses, through mispricing.
BZW, the investment banking arm of Barclays Bank, has been carrying out a review of its business and there is talk that derivatives activity is under the spotlight.
Investment banking is increasingly being seen as expensive, risky and failing to provide the returns that investors demand.

Futures and options are already struggling with a difficult image problem. That is unsurprising, analysts said, in an industry where the legacy of high-profile losses such as those at Barings still lingers.
Britain's oldest merchant bank collapsed in 1995 under the weight of a 1.3 billion dollar loss due to unauthorised derivatives trading.

"There is a greater awareness among senior managers that these things can happen to any large player who takes positions on their books," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at the London Bond Broking Company here.
"You have to build in some allowance for losses, and the investor climate at the moment doesn't make that easy," he said.

If the single currency gets under way on schedule in 1999, it will at a stroke slash the number of derivatives contracts traded in European countries. Instead of individual countries' interest rate and debt futures and options, there will be Europe-wide euro contracts.
But as well as removing business in some contracts, EMU will also shift the focus to others, traders said.

A gilt trader on the LIFFE floor said although volume in gilts and short sterling contracts was still relatively light compared with their German counterparts, companies were unwilling to trim staff levels too low.
"Under a UK out (of EMU) scenario, sterling contract could do huge volumes," he said. "It's not a wise move to have no experienced staff around if that happens."
Lewis said that while attrition was necessary, companies should be clearly focused on new areas which will fill the gaps left.
"Eastern Europe, things like the Czech crown could be very interesting," said Lewis. "The boys down on LIFFE should like that, given the amount of volatility."
